newsitem.title: BURMA: FEATURE - Burma a tempting destination despite boycott.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Burma a tempting destination despite boycott.

text.p: Rudyard Kipling may have done Burma's military government a big favour.
His poem, "The Road to Mandalay" forever immortalised this city and presented a romantic travel destination that has proved too tempting for many tourists to resist.
Despite a travel boycott favoured by charismatic opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi, tourists still flock to Burma to see the mystical land of glittering pagodas and ancient ruins.

The Nobel Peace Prize laureate has urged visitors to stay away, especially during the government's "Visit Myanmar (Burma) Year" that began in November, until the military improves its human rights record and starts talks with the democracy movement.
TOURISTS REACTIONS MIXED OVER BOYCOTT CALLS
Some tourists know about the boycott campaign and come anyway, in an effort to better understand this nation, which is in the process of opening up to the outside world.
"I don't want to give any money to the SLORC," says one American tourist, referring to the ruling military body, the State Law and Order Restoration Council.
Like many travellers, she is well-versed in the political situation and has heard the various arguments in favour of a boycott but has her own reasons for visiting.
"I think if I buy things from people and go to family-run hotels and restaurants I can make sure money gets into the hands of people who need it," she says.
Others do not even know about Suu Kyi's boycott request and see themselves as adventurous travellers out to discover a relatively uncharted land.

Ed Boyer, a 78-year-old tourist from Toronto, Canada, was full of observations about Burma after travelling on his own road to Mandalay in a 20-hour journey on a non-airconditioned train from Rangoon.
But he is not really interested in politics.
"Boycott, no I don't know about any boycott here. What's the boycott about?" he asked.
Boyer says he has heard of Suu Kyi and knew she had been under house arrest but knew little else.
BURMA ACCUSED OF ABUSES IN VISIT MYANMAR YEAR

The SLORC has been attacked by the opposition and human rights groups for spending huge amounts of money on the tourism campaign and for building huge hotels and facilities for tourists while citizens have barely enough to eat.

Some rights groups have also accused the government of using forced labour to fix up some tourist sites for Visit Myanmar Year. The SLORC has urged Burmese people to do all they can to help make the tourism year a success.
This included requiring people to put a new coat of paint on all homes and buildings, regardless of their financial situation.
Burma, renamed "Myanmar" by the SLORC after it seized power in 1988, hopes to attract 250,000 tourists during Visit Myanmar Year.

It is one way the SLORC hopes to attract foreign currency to help a sagging economy. Burma was virtually closed off to the world for more than a quarter of a century during the nationalistic rule of former strongman General Ne Win.

A tourism ministry official says there are no precise figures for tourist visits since Visit Myanmar Year began in November. But tourist arrivals have risen 40 percent between April 1996 and end-February over the same period last year.
COUNTRY OFFERS VARIETY OF TOURIST DESTINATIONS
Mandalay, the last capital of Burma before the British took over in the 19th century, is one of the top tourist destinations along with the ancient ruins of Pagan.
At dusk, the top of the Shwesandaw Paya temple in Pagan's Archaeological Zone seems more like the Tower of Babel than an 11th century relic as tourists chatter and look out over the ruins.
It's sunset, the most awaited part of the day, when visitors hope to get the perfect picture of the sun sinking into the horizon amid a backdrop of centuries old pagodas and stupas.
Tourists laugh and shout in various languages as they struggle up the steep steps of the pagoda to get to the top in time for the sunset.
"It's magnificent," murmured one French tourist as she looked out at some of the 2,200 ruins that dot the landscape. "Imagine what it used to look like."

Romantic sights like the ancient ruins of Pagan, elegant gilded pagodas spread across the country and the natural beauty of Inle Lake in Shan State are enough to entice many to heed the call of Kipling despite the boycott.
